newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Canadian Air cargo seen stable.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Canadian Air cargo seen stable.

text.p: Canadian Airlines International managed to hang on to almost all of its cargo customers through the financial crisis which almost grounded the airline late last year, cargo vice-president Barry Rempell said.
Cargo revenues for the October to December quarter fell less than two percent, but that paled next to the 12 percent decline in passenger and passenger charter revenues.
CAI Cargo even gained traffic as a result of a two-month strike just ending at four Air Canada regional airlines, business it believes it can retain, Rempell said in an interview here last week.

Canadian's financial crisis broke last Nov 1, during peak season for cargo shippers. Rempell said his customers stuck with the airline in part because of market conditions as CAI's demise would have put more freight up or grabs than other carriers could have absorbed.
He says they also stayed with CAI because the airline made it a point to keep large customers briefed about the status of negotiations with employees, government and creditors for concessions.
Before the crisis made the front pages in Canada, CAI had begun special daily briefings for major customers, said Rempell.
"We went out to all of our major customers - before we really went public (with a lot of Canadian's financial troubles) - and said this is the kind of thing that's coming down," he said.
"I believe a lot of our relationships strengthened as a consequence," he said. "One customer told me he was staying with us because he had been there (near bankruptcy) himself."

CAI explained to customers its restructuring plan, which included deferring some expenses, such as aircraft rent payments, until mid-1997. The plan included performance targets, so customers can monitor the progress of the restructing.
Rempell said those targets are being met or exceeded.
"For me, it has been the easiest job in the last three months because we have been consistently outperforming what we had put in that plan," said Rempell.
The crisis helped bring CAI closer to major customers, and focus its attention improving its key account stategy.
As part of the CAI's restructuring, it dropped unprofitable services to Germany and France while increasing flights to the UK.
The airline now has only one route to continental Europe - a Toronto-Rome service shared with Alitalia.
That forced CAI to change how it serves some European cargo customers.
CAI's strategy focuses on routing business from northern Europe through London, using lift from partner British Airways.
Fully 90 percent of its transatlantic business now moves via London, said Rempell.

Oddly, losing Paris as a gateway was most injurious to the carrier's North Italy business, which preferred it to Rome, he said. CAI responded by working with Alitalia to smooth over groundhandling problems in Rome so they could move more freight reliably on their joint flights.
